annotatedSteps.description: Express tan θ and cot θ in terms of sin θ and cos θ and simplify individual fractions
annotatedSteps.studentWork:
LHS = tan θ / (1 - cot θ) + cot θ / (1 - tan θ)
= (sin θ/cos θ) / ((sin θ - cos θ)/sin θ) + (cos θ/sin θ) / ((cos θ - sin θ)/cos θ)
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: ✓ Correct conversion to sin θ and cos θ.

annotatedSteps.description: Simplify denominators and combine fractions with common denominator
annotatedSteps.studentWork:
= sin² θ / (cos θ(sin θ - cos θ)) + cos² θ / (sin θ(sin θ - cos θ))
= (sin³ θ - cos³ θ) / (sin θ cos θ(sin θ - cos θ))
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: ½ Sign slip: factoring out -1 from (cos θ - sin θ) requires changing the '+' between fractions to '-'.
annotatedSteps.correctedWorking: = sin² θ / [cos θ(sin θ - cos θ)] - cos² θ / [sin θ(sin θ - cos θ)] = (sin³ θ - cos³ θ) / [sin θ cos θ(sin θ - cos θ)]

annotatedSteps.description: Factorise numerator using a³ - b³ and simplify to RHS
annotatedSteps.studentWork:
= (sin θ - cos θ)(sin² θ + sin θ cos θ + cos² θ) / (sin θ cos θ(sin θ - cos θ))
= (1 + sin θ cos θ) / (sin θ cos θ) = 1 + sec θ cosec θ = RHS
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: ✓ Correct factorization, cancellation, and simplification to RHS.

Very good algebraic flow and identity usage. Just watch out for the sign change when taking a negative factor out of the denominator.

annotatedSteps.description: Assume rationality and express √3 in terms of integers
annotatedSteps.studentWork:
Let 5 − 2√3 be rational. Then 5 − 2√3 = a/b, where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0.
⇒ 2√3 = 5 − a/b = (5b − a)/b
⇒ √3 = (5b − a)/(2b)

annotatedSteps.description: Establish contradiction and state final conclusion
annotatedSteps.studentWork: Since a and b are integers, (5b − a)/(2b) is rational, but √3 is irrational. This is a contradiction.
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: ½ Contradiction stated, but the explicit final conclusion statement 'Hence, 5 - 2√3 is irrational' is missing.
annotatedSteps.correctedWorking: Since a and b are integers, (5b − a)/(2b) is rational, which contradicts the fact that √3 is irrational. Hence, our assumption was incorrect, and 5 − 2√3 is an irrational number.

results.teacherNote: Marked against: Assuming 5 - 2√3 is rational and rearranging to isolate √3 (1); Arriving at contradiction and stating conclusion that 5 - 2√3 is irrational (1). The algebraic steps and contradiction are spot on. Always finish with the explicit conclusion sentence stating that the given number is irrational.

annotatedSteps.description: Proof of irrationality using method of contradiction
annotatedSteps.studentWork:
1/√5 = 1/2.2360679… = 0.4472135…
The decimal expansion of 1/√5 is non-terminating and non-repeating.
A rational number always has a terminating or repeating decimal expansion.
∴ 1/√5 is an irrational number. Hence proved.
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: × Invalid method: Decimal expansion cannot be assumed or quoted to prove irrationality. A formal proof by contradiction is required.
annotatedSteps.correctedWorking: Let 1/√5 be rational, so 1/√5 = a/b where a and b are coprime integers and b ≠ 0. Then √5 = b/a. Since a and b are integers, b/a is rational, which implies √5 is rational. This contradicts the fact that √5 is irrational. Hence, 1/√5 is an irrational number.

results.teacherNote: Marked against: Assume 1/√5 is rational as a/b (coprime integers / b ≠ 0) (1); Show that 5 divides a² and 5 divides b² / contradicting coprimality (1.5); Conclude that 1/√5 is irrational (0.5). Decimal approximations cannot be used to prove irrationality because stating the expansion is non-terminating and non-repeating assumes the conclusion. Use the standard proof by contradiction. This method does not work in general, so the working built on it cannot earn method marks — use a method that holds in every case.
